title: Instance-specific operational processes exist because generic vault interfaces do not cover every protocol's mechanics
content:
A.6.1.1.6.2.6.1.3.1.1.1.3 reserves a slot in every Instance for "operational procedures or monitoring requirements unique to this Instance that **deviate from or otherwise supplement** the general Pattern Liquidity Layer processes." Maple uses it: `requestMapleRedemption` and `cancelMapleRedemption` are defined here rather than in the shared controller documentation (A.6.1.1.6.2.6.1.3.1.1.1.3.1).

The existence of this slot is an admission with a good design behind it. The coordinator document standardizes what can be standardized — ERC-4626 and ERC-7540 vocabularies, roles, rate limits — but real protocols expose idiosyncratic functions, and forcing them into a generic interface would either lose capability or corrupt the shared abstraction. Localizing the exception keeps the general layer clean while still documenting the specific call an operator must make.

The cancel capability is itself notable: an asynchronous redemption creates a pending state that may need to be undone, so `cancelMapleRedemption` "remov[es] the specified number of shares from the pending redemption." Sync vault standards need no such call.

The two functions treat rate limits differently, and the text is worth reading closely. The request path will "ensure the redemption amount is within the allowed rate limit for the specified vault **and decrease the rate limit** for the redemption amount." The cancel path only "check[s] that a rate limit exists for the asset" — no restoration of the consumed capacity is specified. With Maple's withdrawal limit set to Unlimited this has no present effect, but the same pattern applied to a bounded outflow limit would let request-then-cancel cycles erode exit capacity.
description: Maple needs bespoke requestMapleRedemption and cancelMapleRedemption calls beyond the shared ERC-4626 and ERC-7540 vocabulary, including the ability to withdraw a pending redemption request.
